note: Project-local source inventory. The repository root evidence policy remains controlling; source class and operational states are separate. For a historical source served through a modern digital presentation, evidenceClass describes the underlying source when stated, while accessState and rightsState describe what is actually accessed and can be reused.

sources.title: Melodie-register of the 2005 critical edition, printed pp. 663-664
sources.type: Index of printed tune directions and the texts sung to them, in the copyrighted critical edition
supports: 'Un jour m'en alloit &c.' is the printed direction for texts 27 and 56
'Prendete la' and item 9's incipit 'Gy laat, dien gy vind rede staan' both key the same pair of texts, 9 and 32
't En is niet alle tijd, &c.' is the direction for texts 41 and 57
Text 131, 's Heeren heerlijckheyts loff, is directed to Psalm 6
Texts 34, 35 and 52 share Gavotte. A la fronté, On-herroepelijcke jeugd and Soet Geselschap dat met my
limits: It is an index of direction STRINGS, not a catalogue of melodies: two poems under one heading did not necessarily share a tune. The apparatus note on item 56 says the melody there is unknown and is not text 27's, while the register files 27 and 56 together. Cite the register for 'same direction', never for 'same melody'.

Several texts are keyed by the incipit of another poem (item 9's first line keys texts 9 and 32), so a second string is usually a second key, not a second tune. This is the shape of the old 'Bourgeois or psalm 42' false dichotomy.
Copyrighted: only the entries this project uses may be transcribed, as bibliographic facts; never the register wholesale.

Poems often written on Sundays, as relaxation after the sermon (p. 646)

sources.title: Psalmen en Gezangen (Hervormde Bundel 1938), Gezang 75, p. 501, nr. 239
sources.type: Reference to the printed hymnal as catalogued by the Dutch Song Database
supports: Gezang 75 stands on printed p. 501 of the 1938 bundel, its incipit is «'t Oog omhoog, het hart naar boven», and the melody is credited to Louis Bourgeois
limits: The printed bundel has not been collated; the page number and the melody credit come from the database rendering, and the database is offline.

sources.title: Gezang 75 — public reproduction of the 1938 text in modernised spelling
sources.type: Third-party web reproduction of a protected hymnal text
supports: That the 1938 reworking runs to three stanzas and that its third stanza descends from 1676 stanza X ('Ah! dat aller menschen tongen')
limits: Modernised spelling and a private site: no collation, no critical apparatus, not a witness for the printed page.

sources.title: The Genevan Psalter — the psalm 42 melody and its composers
sources.type: Scholarly survey of the Genevan psalter (Revue Chretiens, Societes, Journal)
supports: That the melodies for Beze's psalm paraphrases, including psalm 42 «Ainsi qu'on oit le cerf bruire», were written by Loys Bourgeois
limits: Seen in a search rendering while checking the Bourgeois attribution; the article itself has not been read in full, and no page is cited.

sources.title: Critical-edition item 27 — Den eersten psalm uytgebreydet, p. 120 (the 'Un jour' the apparatus excludes)
sources.type: Critical edition, text of the item that carries the other 'Un jour' tune direction
supports: Item 27, Psalm 1 expanded, stands on p. 120 under the direction 'Te singen op de wijse: Un jour m'en alloit &c.'; the apparatus identifies that melody as the French chanson 'Un jour m'en allais seulette' by Grouzy (d. 1568), printed in the Quinzieme livre de chansons, Paris 1571
limits: Copyrighted apparatus: paraphrased, not quoted at length. Identifies the tune that our poem does NOT use — it says nothing about what our poem's own tune was.

sources.title: Claes Stapel, Het lust-hof der zielen (Alkmaar: Jacob Pietersz. Moerbeek, 1681) — the reprint at printed p. 495
sources.type: Digital diplomatic presentation of the 1681 anthology
supports: That the poem was reprinted in 1681 by Claes Stapel on printed p. 495 under the heading 'Heemels heerlijkheids lof. Voiz: Un jour, &c.', with the incipit 'Hoog! om hoog! mijn ziel naa booven'
limits: The DBNL transcription of this two-column anthology interleaves the columns, so only the heading, the tune direction, the incipit and the page number can be relied on until the page image is seen.
The editor of the anthology is Claes Stapel, not Hendrick Stapel: the earlier research and the copy carried the wrong first name.

sources.title: gezangboek.nl — Psalm 42 page listing the hymns sung to that melody
sources.type: Private reference site mapping hymns to melodies
supports: Independent support for the melody identity: 'Hoog omhoog, het hart naar boven' (Lodenstein) is listed among the hymns sung to the psalm 42 melody, together with Datheen's 'Als een hert gejaagd, o Heere'
limits: A hobby reference site, seen through a search rendering, not opened; secondary and not citable for anything but the association itself.

sources.title: «Свете тихий» — Православная энциклопедия, т. 62, с. 54–55 (свящ. Михаил Желтов)
sources.type: Scholarly encyclopaedia article on the hymn, its rite position, transmission and bibliography
supports: The hymn is a fixed part of Vespers in all post-iconoclast Byzantine monastic Typika and is not omitted even at Pascha, while the Hagia Sophia cathedral rite did not have it
It stands in the earliest Palestinian Horologia; many manuscripts and editions, including the modern Russian Horologion, ascribe it to Sophronius of Jerusalem
The attribution to Sophronius is probably wrong because the hymn already appears in a 6th–7th century papyrus, P. Lond. 2037B (Tripolitis 1970)
Basil, De Spiritu Sancto 73, is understood by ancient and modern authors alike as referring to this hymn, and quotes the Trinitarian formula 'We praise Father and Son and the Holy Spirit of God'
The attribution to Athenogenes arose from conflating two distinct testimonies in Basil
The hymn falls into three parts: Christological, Trinitarian, and Christological again
The opening has a parallel in the ancient acclamation Φῶς ἀγαθόν before a lamp (Varro, De lingua Latina VI 4), a derivation some scholars reject
limits: A secondary encyclopaedia article, not a critical edition: it reports the papyrus and the manuscript position without printing an apparatus
It does NOT ascribe the hymn to the Apostolic Constitutions; the widespread 'first recorded in the Apostolic Constitutions VIII.35' is therefore not supported by the source read here and is held open
The papyrus itself was not seen; only the article's report of it

sources.title: Basil of Caesarea, De Spiritu Sancto 29.73 — NPNF translation (Schaff)
sources.type: Primary patristic text in a public-domain English translation
supports: The fathers did not receive the evening light in silence but gave thanks at its appearing
The author of the lamp-lighting thanksgiving is unknown to Basil ('Who was the author of these words of thanksgiving at the lighting of the lamps, we are not able to say')
The people utter 'the ancient form', and the quoted formula is 'We praise Father, Son, and God's Holy Spirit'
The Hymn of Athenogenes is mentioned as a different thing, in the following sentence
limits: Read in the NPNF English translation (§ 73 and the opening of §§ 74–75); the Greek was not collated
This proves that the hymn existed and was called ancient c. 375, not when it was composed

sources.title: ChoralWiki (CPDL), 'Phos Hilaron' — Greek text and translations
sources.type: Community choral library page carrying the Greek text and English versions
supports: The six-line received Greek text used for the translation
The existence of an English verse tradition and of the Church Slavonic 'Svyete tikhii'
The hymn is an evening hymn sung at the lighting of the lamps
limits: A community transcription, not an edition: it carries no apparatus and no manuscript sigla
The Greek text is public domain and is reproduced as text; the page's editorial matter is not reproduced
A printed Greek Horologion or a critical edition (Plank 2001) has not been collated — that is what LOCATOR_HOLD records

sources.title: Азбука веры, статья «Свете Тихий» — церковнославянский текст, русский перевод, толкование
sources.type: Popular Orthodox reference site; carries a Russian prose translation of the hymn
supports: A Russian prose translation of the hymn circulates: 'О Отрадный Свет святой славы Бессмертного Отца Небесного, Святого Блаженного, Иисус Христос!…'
The Church Slavonic word 'тихий' in this hymn was understood as 'исполненный светлой радости'
limits: Read as a search excerpt, not as a full page: quotes above are the excerpt's wording
Popular reference, not a scholarly source; the translator of the Russian text is not named on the excerpt
Used to establish that a Russian prose translation exists, never as the source of our wording

sources.title: Московская Сретенская духовная академия, «Песнопение вечерни „Свете Тихий“: богословско-филологический комментарий»
sources.type: Seminary commentary with a working Russian translation of the hymn
supports: A second independent Russian prose translation exists: 'Иисусе Христе, Тихий (ясный, радостный) Свет святой славы Бессмертнаго Отца Небеснаго, Святаго Блаженнаго!…'
ἱλαρόν is glossed with a range that includes 'мягкий, снисходительный, тишайший' and, elsewhere, 'яркий, золотистый, радостный'
limits: Read as a search excerpt, not as a full page
A teaching text, not an edition; some of its renderings are explanatory paraphrases ('голосами святых людей') rather than the sense of αἴσιαι

sources.title: Л. Яцкевич, «Свете тихий… Заметки литературоведа» (Русская линия, 2018) — цитирует переложение К. Бальмонта
sources.type: Literary essay quoting a Russian poetic reworking of the hymn
supports: The Church Slavonic 'Свете тихий' is described as a translation from the Greek original of one of the earliest hymns of the early Church
Konstantin Balmont made an artistic reworking of the prayer, quoted with a repeated refrain 'Свете тихий, сияй нам, сияй нам, Свете тихий, сияй без конца'
limits: Only the opening of the essay was read
Balmont's text is a paraphrase with an added refrain, not a translation; it is recorded so that nobody mistakes it for one, and it is not used

sources.title: Apostolic Constitutions, Book VIII §§34–37 — ANF translation (Schaff), newadvent.org
sources.type: Primary liturgical text in a public-domain English translation
supports: VIII.34 prescribes the hours of prayer including evening
VIII.35 orders the evening assembly and 'the repetition of the psalm at the lighting up the lights'
VIII.36 is the deacon's bidding prayer for the evening
VIII.37 is the bishop's evening thanksgiving ('O God, who art without beginning and without end…')
Not one line of Φῶς ἱλαρόν occurs in VIII.34–37 — the Constitutions give the rite, not the text of the hymn
sources.limits: Read only in the NPNF English translation; the Greek was not collated. Chapters were read in the sequence VIII.34–37 and XLII–XLV, not the whole book.

sources.title: British Library Archives and Manuscripts catalogue, Royal MS 1 D VII (Codex Alexandrinus, vol. 3)
sources.type: Library catalogue description of a manuscript volume
supports: Volume 3 of the codex carries Athanasius's letter to Marcellinus and Psalms to Ecclesiasticus
The canticles listed are Magnificat, Nunc dimittis, Benedictus and the Ὕμνος Ἑωθινός (Gloria in excelsis)
Φῶς ἱλαρόν is not listed among them
sources.limits: A catalogue description, not a page-by-page collation; absence is established from the list of contents, not from an autopsy.

sources.title: 'Book of Odes (Bible)' — survey of the Greek ode collections and of Codex Alexandrinus
sources.type: Encyclopaedia article, read as a search excerpt
supports: The earliest surviving collection of odes is in the 5th-century Codex Alexandrinus: 14 odes after the Psalter
The 14th ode is the Gloria in Excelsis (Canticle of the Early Morning) — the last in the collection
sources.limits: Read as a search excerpt; used only to confirm the constituents of the Alexandrinus ode collection. Not a critical edition.

sources.title: Oxyrhynchus hymn, P.Oxy. XV 1786 — datings and description (search excerpts, 2025 reporting)
sources.type: Popular reporting on a papyrus, read as excerpts; papyrological edition not consulted
supports: P.Oxy. XV 1786 carries a Christian hymn with Greek vocal notation, dated c. 250–300
It is fragmentary: the text survives with lacunae
sources.limits: The editio princeps (Grenfell–Hunt, 1922) and the musical bibliography were not read. The dating is reported, not checked palaeographically. Used only to place Φῶς ἱλαρόν in the order of witnesses, never in copy.

sources.title: Odes of Solomon — date, language and manuscripts (survey article, read as excerpts)
sources.type: Encyclopaedia article, read as a search excerpt
supports: A collection of 42 odes, most scholars dating the composition c. 70–125
Preserved chiefly in Syriac manuscripts of the 10th–15th centuries, with a Greek fragment (P. Bodmer XI, 3rd–4th c.)
sources.limits: Read as a search excerpt; Charlesworth/Lattke editions were not consulted. Used only to establish that an older Christian hymn corpus exists, never in copy.

sources.title: Apostolic Constitutions, Book VII §47 — morning prayer («Glory be to God in the highest…»), ANF translation
sources.type: Primary liturgical text in a public-domain English translation
supports: VII.47 is headed 'A Morning Prayer' and opens 'Glory be to God in the highest, and upon earth peace, good-will among men' (Luke 2:14)
It continues 'We praise You, we sing hymns to You, we bless You; we glorify You, we worship You by Your great High Priest…'
VII.48 is the evening prayer; VII.49 the prayer at dinner
So the Greek Gloria does appear in the Apostolic Constitutions — unlike Φῶς ἱλαρόν, which does not
sources.limits: Read in the NPNF English translation only; the Greek was not collated. Only VII.47–49 were read, not the whole book.

sources.title: 'Sub tuum praesidium' — survey of the Greek text, the Rylands papyrus 470 and the dating dispute
sources.type: Encyclopaedia article, read in full
supports: The earliest text is Greek, Ὑπὸ τὴν σὴν εὐσπλαγχνίαν, found in a Coptic Christmas liturgy
Rylands Papyrus 470 was dated to the 3rd century by Lobel and to the 4th by Roberts
Förster dates the papyrus to the 8th century and states there is no consensus for Lobel's date; Towarek concludes the earliest textual witness is 6th–7th century
The hymn is identified in the Georgian Iadgari of Jerusalem, i.e. in liturgical use in the 5th century
Ancient versions exist in Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Latin
sources.limits: The article was read, the underlying studies (Förster, Towarek) were not. The dating is therefore reported as a dispute, with both sides named, not resolved here.

sources.title: 'Te Deum' — authorship, date and liturgical history
sources.type: Encyclopaedia article, read as the first section
supports: A Latin hymn traditionally dated before AD 500, almost certainly of the 4th century, of uncertain authorship
Attribution to Ambrose is unlikely; the 19th-century attribution to Nicetas of Remesiana was shown to be spurious by Kähler (1958)
In Benedictine use from the 6th century; preserved in the 8th-century Frankish Hymnal
sources.limits: Read as an article, not as an edition; the critical literature (Kähler) was not consulted. The Latin text was not collated.

sources.title: «Η Μεγάλη Δοξολογία» — греческий богослужебный текст Великого славословия
sources.type: Энциклопедическая статья с полным богослужебным текстом
supports: Полный греческий текст Великого славословия, восемь первых строк — собственно гимн
Дальше в последовании идут псалмические стихи («Καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν…», «Κύριε, καταφυγὴ ἐγενήθης ἡμῖν…»), Трисвятое и «Δόξα Πατρὶ καὶ Υἱῷ»
Малого славословия текст короче и совпадает с первыми строками Великого
Великое славословие поётся в конце утрени перед Литургией по Октоиху
sources.limits: Текст взят из энциклопедической статьи, не из печатной Минеи или Часослова; `LOCATOR_HOLD`. Греческая орфография в статье местами монотоническая.

sources.title: Латинские переложения Φῶς ἱλαρόν — `Lumen hilare` и `Iucunda lux tu gloriae` (форумные и блоговые свидетельства)
sources.type: Форумное обсуждение и блог, ссылающиеся на аннотацию компакт-диска; не научный источник
supports: `Lumen hilare` — буквальный латинский перевод, известный по собранию Adrian Fortescue, Latin Hymns (нач. XX в.)
`Iucunda lux tu gloriae` — метрическое переложение в четырёх строфах, происхождение не установлено
Его поют на напев `Jesu dulcis memoria`; «григорианизированную» мелодию приписывают Дом Люсьену Давиду (первая половина XX в.)
Один из участников обсуждения утверждает, что латинского богослужебного употребления у этого гимна не было вовсе
sources.limits: Источник уровня D: форум и блог. Ни Фортескью, ни Давид по печатным изданиям не сверены. Использован только для того, чтобы **не** заявлять древность латинской версии; ни одно положительное утверждение на нём не строится.
